name: MOGS-CDG (congenital disorder of glycosylation type IIb)

clinicalPearls: MOGS encodes endoplasmic reticulum mannosyl-oligosaccharide glucosidase (glucosidase I), which removes the outermost terminal alpha-1,2-linked glucose from the newly transferred N-glycan, the first trimming step of glycan processing.
It is therefore classified as a type II CDG (a processing or trimming defect) rather than an assembly defect.
A crucial diagnostic trap is that serum transferrin isoelectric focusing is typically normal, because the defect does not alter the sialylation-dependent charge that this test detects.
Diagnosis instead rests on urine oligosaccharide analysis, which shows a characteristic glucose-rich tetrasaccharide derived from the unprocessed precursor.
The clinical picture is a severe neonatal multisystem disorder with dysmorphism, generalised hypotonia, seizures, feeding difficulty and hepatomegaly.
Hypogammaglobulinaemia is characteristic, yet a paradoxical relative resistance to certain enveloped viruses has been described because their envelope glycoproteins depend on glucosylated N-glycans.
Multisystem neurological and hepatic involvement usually dominates the clinical course despite the immunological abnormality.
reference.pathophysiology: MOGS (glucosidase I) catalyses the first step in processing of the N-linked oligosaccharide after it is transferred en bloc onto nascent glycoproteins in the endoplasmic reticulum, cleaving the terminal alpha-1,2-glucose from the triglucosylated precursor Glc3Man9GlcNAc2. This trimming is required for entry into the calnexin and calreticulin quality-control cycle and for orderly glycoprotein folding and onward processing. Loss of function leaves glycoproteins bearing unprocessed, still-glucosylated glycans, disrupts protein folding and quality control, and causes accumulation and urinary excretion of glucose-rich oligosaccharides. Because the sialylation of transferrin is unaffected, the standard transferrin screening test remains normal, which is the principal reason the disorder is missed. Inheritance is autosomal recessive.
additionalDifferentials: Other type II CDGs (for example MGAT2, B4GALT1, SLC35 transporter and COG-complex defects)
Type I CDGs presenting with neonatal hypotonia and seizures
Peroxisomal disorders with neonatal hypotonia and hepatopathy
Other syndromic neonatal encephalopathies with dysmorphism
additionalInvestigations: Urine oligosaccharide analysis for the characteristic glucose-rich tetrasaccharide (key confirmatory test)
Serum transferrin isoelectric focusing (characteristically normal, which supports rather than excludes the diagnosis)
MOGS molecular genetic testing via a CDG panel or exome sequencing
Immunoglobulin levels and functional immune assessment
Liver function tests and hepatic imaging
Glucosidase I enzyme activity assay in a specialist laboratory
redFlags: Neonatal seizures with encephalopathy and feeding failure
Serious or recurrent bacterial infection in the setting of hypogammaglobulinaemia
Apnoea or respiratory compromise in a hypotonic neonate
reference.prognosis: Reported cases have generally followed a severe course with death in early infancy, although the full phenotypic range is still being defined as more affected individuals are identified.
pitfalls: Excluding a CDG because transferrin isoelectric focusing is normal, the classic way MOGS-CDG is overlooked
Failing to request urine oligosaccharide analysis in a hypotonic dysmorphic neonate
Attributing recurrent infection solely to a primary immunodeficiency without considering a glycosylation disorder
Misinterpreting the urinary oligosaccharide pattern as a lysosomal storage disorder
references: Congenital disorders of glycosylation review literature
